title: Console-driven JSON Mode pilot overview with Sable Ventures
summary: Intro demo and pilot kickoff for Redwood's Console JSON Mode, focused on schema-driven structured output, tool calling, guardrails & Optimize recommendations. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for PII workloads; next steps include pilot SOW, security packet, and benchmark runbook.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-16 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (Sable CTO), Rina (Head of ML), Marcus (Infra), Tess (PM)

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. quick agenda, i want to run the console JSON mode sandbox, show schema enforcement, then maya will deep dive on safe tool calling and optimize suggestions, and we'll close with pilot scope and security Qs. sound good?
[00:18] Liam: yep, sounds good. we only have about an hour so appreciate the brevity.
[00:25] Rina: couple things from our side — we want strong structured outputs for our data ingestion and a safe way for the model to call internal services, and we need to see how fallback behavior looks when a tool errors.
[00:42] Maya: totally, that's exactly what we'll demo. just to set context, are you planning hosted or private for the pilot? any PII constraints?
[00:51] Liam: pilot likely private within our VPC; some of our datasets are sensitive so we need KMS + audit logs. but we're open to starting hosted if it's faster to iterate.
[01:05] Samir: that's a pattern we see — start hosted for speed then move to private/dedicated once SLOs and security are signed off. for the pilot i recommend private control plane with dedicated inference nodes if you want consistent latency.
[01:22] Marcus: can you explain the difference again between dedicated and private? we heard both terms but not sure.
[01:28] Maya: sure — Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity in our cloud offering; Private means the control plane and data plane live inside your network (VPC or on-prem). Dedicated can be in a private deployment too, but often customers choose Private + Dedicated for strict data residency / compliance.
[01:50] Tess: got it. can you show the console? we want to see the schema contracts part.
[01:57] Samir: jumping in — opening the console, under JSON Mode -> Contracts -> new contract.
[02:10] [screen share noise, background typing]
[02:18] Maya: here we define the output schema — we'll create a claim object with fields: claim_id (string), claimant (object), amount (number), validated (boolean), actions (array of actions). note: the console allows required/optional rules and multiple fallbacks.
[02:40] Rina: will the model ever hallucinate fields that aren't in the schema?
[02:45] Maya: the runtime enforces output contracts; we run a validation layer post-response. if the model returns extra fields we strip them, if required fields are missing we can trigger a re-ask or route to a fallback parser or a tool that extracts KV cache entries.
[03:05] Liam: show an example of re-ask vs fallback?
[03:10] Maya: sure — i'll trigger a deliberate incomplete response.
[03:18] [demo]
[03:26] Maya: so here the model returned no claimant.name. console shows validation fail, and per route policy we have three-tier fallback: 1) re-ask with clarified prompt, 2) call internal scrapers tool for claimant metadata, 3) safe default rejection with audit tag. you can tune that in the routing/rollout pane.
[03:51] Marcus: when you call internal tools, how is authentication handled? we can't expose secrets to the model process.
[03:58] Maya: good question — tool calls happen in the control plane; secrets are fetched on-demand via your KMS/HSM integration and never embedded in prompts. we support short-lived tokens and role-based access. audit logs capture every call and response.
[04:18] [05:00] Samir: on Optimize — this is where we recommend batching sizes, quantization profiles, and KV cache configs for your workload. maya, show the Optimize recommendations for a claims ingestion workload.
[05:10] Maya: opening Optimize -> workload profiler. we uploaded sample prompt traces earlier, and the profiler suggests a batching window of 30ms with dynamic batching up to 16 tokens per batch, use 4-bit quant for embed-only endpoints, and enable prefix KV caching for repeated claimant metadata. expected cost savings around 38% with similar latency.
[05:40] Rina: 38% sounds great. what about quality regressions with quantization?
[05:47] Maya: we flag potential regression risks and provide regression tests tied to your prompt set. you can auto-run evals after applying a quant profile. for anything risky we recommend A/B rollout with automatic rollback if evals fall below threshold.
[06:10] Liam: do you support function/tool calling where the model picks which internal service to call? we want the model to decide between database lookup, enrichment service, or manual review queue.
[06:21] Maya: yes — that's a primary use case. we map tool schemas into the contract system. the model returns a typed action like {"tool":"db_lookup","args":{"claim_id":"123"}} and the runtime validates the args against the tool schema before executing. the console shows a sandbox-run where the tool was executed in dry-run mode.
[06:45] [06:55] Tess: what happens if a tool throws an unexpected error? we need safe degradation to manual queue.
[07:01] Maya: you can set fallback chains per tool: on transient errors retry, on permission errors escalate to manual review and tag the trace. everything is logged for forensics.
[07:15] Marcus: curious about latency — if the model chains multiple tool calls, what's the expectation?
[07:21] Maya: dependent on tool response times and routing. for low-latency needs we recommend keeping critical lookups in-memory/authed within the same VPC and enabling async tool calls with optimistic responses. the runtime supports streaming incremental responses while background tools run to keep the UI snappy.
[07:46] Rina: you mentioned KV cache — can you explain how prefix cache works?
[07:51] Maya: prefix/KV cache stores repeated key-value decodes across requests, so if claimant metadata is common, subsequent generations hit the cache and skip re-computation. cache invalidation policies are pluggable — TTL, version tags, or event-driven clears.
[08:14] Liam: security packet? can you walk the high-level certs and audit pieces?
[08:21] Samir: sure — we sent a redacted security packet earlier, but in short: SOC2 type II, ISO 27001 in flight, support for customer-managed KMS, SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC in Console, and detailed audit logs with retention tuning. maya will attach the network diagrams and logs schema.
[08:44] Maya: note for private deployments we can integrate with your SIEM and forward audit streams via syslog or secure API endpoints.
[08:56] [09:05] Rina: on data retention, can we make sure PII gets redacted from logs? we need selective masking.
[09:12] Maya: yes — there are configurable redaction policies at ingestion and in trace exports. you can also opt out of request/response storage for certain routes.
[09:28] Liam: okay good. let's talk about pilot success criteria — Rina, do you have metrics?
[09:35] Rina: primary is structured extraction accuracy > 95% on canonical prompts, end-to-end latency < 350ms p50, and cost per processed claim under $0.08. also secure handling of PII and reproducible audit trails.
[09:53] Samir: those are reasonable. we'll map to a 3-week pilot: week 1 onboarding & security review, week 2 benchmark runs and tuning, week 3 evaluation & handoff.
[10:05] Tess: sample data — any constraints on format?
[10:09] Maya: CSV/ndjson with prompt/response pairs is easiest. if you have attachments like PDFs we can provide OCR guidance; we also support structured doc ingestion via attachments in the console.
[10:22] [10:40] Demo: tool chaining example
[10:46] Maya: here's a simulated flow — user submits claim, model returns a JSON action to call enrichment service, enrichment returns additional fields, then model returns final validated object. you'll see the console trace with each action and validation step.
[11:20] Liam: sometimes we need business logic that runs before tool call, can we insert pre-hooks?
[11:26] Maya: absolutely — webhooks/pre-hooks are supported, and you can run sandboxed functions (JS or WASM) as part of the pipeline before invoking external tools.
[11:40] Marcus: how about rate limits and quotas? we have bursty traffic at month-end.
[11:46] Samir: dedicated capacity helps here — you can set autoscale policies and burst allowances. Optimize also suggests burst buffer sizing based on historical traces.
[12:05] Rina: one more question on rollback strategies for model upgrades.
[12:08] Maya: console supports canary rollouts by traffic split and automatic rollback if eval metrics drop. you can pin versions per route.
[12:18] [12:25] Tess: any gotchas migrating our existing heuristics to model-driven toolflow? we have many hand-coded rules.
[12:32] Maya: common approach is hybrid: keep critical heuristics as pre-filters, and use model outputs to enrich or route. Redwood's routing rules let you fallback to heuristics when confidence is low.
[12:48] Liam: you're talking about confidence — does the runtime expose confidence scores?
[12:52] Maya: we expose model logprobs, token-level scores, and an aggregated confidence estimate per contract. you can tune thresholds in the Console.
[13:05] [13:20] Samir: quick note on pricing — hosted per-token + embeddings; Dedicated reserved capacity has monthly commit tiers with predictable unit economics. we'll send example tiers tailored to your expected throughput.
[13:34] Rina: can you show the pilot SOW template?
[13:38] Samir: pulling it up, it's a standard three-week pilot with objectives, acceptance criteria, and responsibilities. core deliverables: security review, benchmark runbook, tuned inference profile, and a final report.
[13:54] [14:10] Live Q&A and interruption: background dog barking briefly, minor crosstalk
[14:25] Marcus: small nit — are we allowed to bring our own models? we want to run a fine-tuned variant we host.
[14:31] Maya: yes — you can bring a model image (container) for Private deployments, or bring weights for Dedicated where we host the runtime. we also support connecting to your model endpoints via external provider bindings.
[14:50] Liam: what about model variant fallback when capacity is saturated?
[14:56] Maya: smart routing can fallback to a smaller quantized variant or a different region. you'll see performance profiles in the model catalog.
[15:12] Tess: demo wrap — can you summarize the pilot scope and deliverables?
[15:18] Samir: sure: 1) security review and KMS onboarding, 2) ingest sample prompts and run baseline benchmark, 3) apply Optimize recommendations and run regression tests, 4) validate contract accuracy and tool chains, 5) final report & next-phase proposal.
[15:39] Rina: timeline ok. are there any blockers from Redwood side?
[15:44] Samir: none major; maya will attach detailed runbook and security packet, and we'll need Marcus to enable peering and share network contact.
[16:00] [16:18] Quick nerves about latency on nested tool calls — maya reassured them with streaming and async patterns
[16:35] [17:05] Pricing nuance: Samir clarified difference between per-token and reserved commit math with examples — customer noted they'd want a spreadsheet example.
[17:28] Samir: we'll include a cost model spreadsheet with ranges for hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[17:38] Tess: ok sounds good. any other open questions?
[17:45] Liam: just one — can you run an initial bench against 500 sample prompts next week?
[17:51] Maya: yes, if you share the prompts we'll kick off the profiler.
[17:58] [closing minutes — recap and confirmation of next steps]
[18:10] Samir: recap — i'll send SOW and pricing; maya to send security + runbook; rina/marcus to provide sample prompts and infra contact. schedule pilot sync for 2026-03-30.
[18:30] Rina: thanks everyone.
[18:34] Liam: thanks, bye.
[18:36] End of recording

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attributions (Samir/Maya overlap), some technical terms slightly garbled (KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash), minor filler words present, timestamps approximate.
